title: Candle Making: Safe Production of Container, Pillar and Event Candles
subtitle: Melt wax safely, make well-wicked container, pillar and small candles, and cost, label and sell them with confidence.
description: A hands-on course for women who want to make candles at home and sell them. You will learn how candles burn, melt wax safely in a double boiler, choose and test wicks, make jar, pillar, tealight and decorative candles, blend scent and colour, fix common faults, and write honest labels and prices for your market.
outcomes: Set up a safe melting area and respond correctly to a wax fire
Choose and burn test wicks, recording melt pool, flame and smoke
Make container, pillar, tealight and layered candles using calculated wax and fragrance weights
Blend fragrances in parts, colour wax with candle dye and fix common faults with evidence
Write an honest label with tested burn time and safety instructions
Cost a batch in naira, set retail and wholesale prices and take payment safely
audience: Women with no candle-making experience who want to make quality candles at home and sell them to households, gift buyers, events, churches and hotels.
tools: Large pot and a stainless steel pouring jug for a double boiler, used only for candles
Digital kitchen scale reading in 1 g steps and a candle or kitchen thermometer
Container wax and pillar grade wax, pre-tabbed and pillar wicks, wick stickers and wick holders
Heat-resistant candle jars, tealight cups and one pillar mould with mould sealer putty
Candle fragrance oils with their Safety Data Sheets, and candle dye
A metal lid that fits your pot, oven gloves, and a fire blanket if available
Smartphone with a calculator, Canva and WhatsApp Business

modules.title: Candle Science and Safety
modules.overview: Understand how a candle burns, which wax to choose, and how to melt wax safely at home. Then learn to fix and burn test wicks so every candle you sell burns cleanly and evenly.

lessons.title: How a candle burns, and how to set up a safe wax workspace
objectives: Explain how wax, wick and flame work together in plain words
Compare paraffin, soy, palm and beeswax for different candle types
Set up a double boiler and a safe melting area at home
Respond correctly if hot wax catches fire

blocks.text: A candle is a small fuel system. The **wax** is the fuel, the **wick** is the pump, and the **flame** is the engine. When you light the wick, the heat melts a little wax around it into a shallow liquid called the **melt pool**. The wick soaks up that liquid wax and carries it upward, the same way a cloth soaks up water. This movement through tiny gaps in the wick is called **capillary action**.

Near the top of the wick the heat turns the liquid wax into a hot gas (vapour). That gas mixes with oxygen from the air and burns, giving light, heat, water vapour and carbon dioxide. The heat then melts more wax, and the cycle continues on its own. The National Candle Association explains that all waxes are mostly hydrogen and carbon, which is why they burn this way. If the cycle is broken, for example the wick is too thin to carry enough wax or the flame cannot get enough air, the candle smokes, shrinks or goes out.

blocks.name: candle
blocks.alt: A lit candle with a steady flame
blocks.caption: A steady, teardrop flame means wax, wick and air are in balance.

blocks.title: The burning cycle
items: Flame heats wax
Melt pool forms
Wick draws wax up
Wax turns to vapour
Vapour burns with oxygen
blocks.caption: Each step feeds the next, so a candle keeps burning until the wax or wick runs out.

blocks.text: Reading the flame

Look closely at a lit candle and you will see colours. The blue part at the bottom is where wax vapour starts to break apart. The bright yellow part is glowing carbon particles: this is where most of the light comes from. The thin outer edge is the hottest part. A flicker that sends up black smoke means some carbon escaped without burning. In your own candles, regular smoke is a sign that something is wrong, usually a wick that is too big or too long, or a draught.
The four waxes you will meet

head: Wax
Where it comes from
Best use for a beginner
Things to know
rows: Sold in grades for containers (softer) and pillars (harder). Widely available and usually cheapest.
Soft, so most soy wax is made for jars, not freestanding candles. Can show white 'frosting' on the surface.
Hard wax that can set with a crystal or feather pattern. Ask your supplier for the grade.
Has its own honey smell and natural colour. Usually costs more and needs a larger wick.

blocks.text: Every wax is sold with a recommended melting, fragrance and pouring temperature. These differ from product to product, so always ask your supplier for the **product data sheet** and keep it in your notebook. Use a thermometer every time. Guessing temperature by eye is the main reason beginners get bad results and the main way kitchens get burnt.
Setting up a safe workspace

items: Choose a stable table or counter away from curtains, gas cylinders and anything that can burn. Keep the floor clear so you cannot trip while carrying hot wax.

Use a **double boiler**: a large pot with some water, and a metal pouring jug or smaller pot of wax standing inside it. The water stops the wax from getting hotter than boiling water, which protects the wax and lowers the fire risk.
Never put a pot of wax directly on a gas flame, kerosene stove or hot plate, and never leave melting wax unattended, not even for a quick phone call or to answer the gate.
Keep the water level topped up so the outer pot never boils dry, and keep water out of the wax: water in hot wax spits and can burn you.
Keep a metal lid that fits your pot, a fire blanket if you can get one, and oven gloves within arm's reach before you switch on the heat.
Keep children and pets out of the room while wax is hot.

blocks.title: If wax catches fire
blocks.text: Turn off the heat if you can do it safely. Smother the flames by sliding a metal lid or fire blanket over the pot and leave it covered until it is completely cold. **Never pour water on a wax fire**: the water turns to steam instantly and throws burning wax out of the pot. Do not try to carry the burning pot outside. If the fire is not out at once, get everyone out of the house and call for help.

Overheated wax gives warnings before it catches fire. If you see smoke rising from the wax itself, or smell a sharp burning smell, switch off the heat straight away and let it cool. This is why the thermometer matters: if your wax is near the temperature on the data sheet, you are working far below the danger zone.

blocks.title: Worked example: setting up in a small kitchen
blocks.context: For example, Chiamaka in Owerri has a two-burner gas cooker, a 5 litre pot, a 1 litre stainless steel jug and one hour while her children are at school.
steps: She clears the counter next to the cooker, moves the kitchen curtain out of the way, and puts the pot lid and a dry towel nearby.
She pours water into the big pot until it reaches about one third of the way up the jug, so the jug cannot float or tip.
She weighs 500 g of container wax into the jug and places the jug in the water, then lights the burner on medium.
She clips her thermometer to the jug and checks it every few minutes, stirring gently with a metal spoon.
When the doorbell rings, she switches off the burner before going to the gate, then relights it when she returns.
blocks.result: Her wax melts evenly to the temperature on her data sheet, no water gets into the wax, and the cooker is never left burning without her.

blocks.title: Dedicated tools
blocks.text: Keep your candle pots, jugs and spoons only for candle work. Wax and fragrance oil are hard to clean off completely, and they do not belong in food.

takeaways: A candle burns because the wick carries melted wax up to the flame, where it turns to vapour and burns
Paraffin, soy, palm and beeswax behave differently, so follow each supplier's data sheet
Always melt wax in a double boiler with a thermometer, and never leave it unattended
Smother a wax fire with a lid or fire blanket, never water

activity.title: Build your safe melting station
steps: Choose your work spot and remove anything that can burn within easy reach of the cooker
Assemble your double boiler and check the jug stands steady in the water
Place a fitting metal lid, oven gloves and thermometer beside the cooker
Write your fire plan in three lines on a card: heat off, cover with lid, never water
Stick the card on the wall near your cooker
activity.evidence: A photo of your set-up with the lid, gloves, thermometer and fire plan card visible

lessons.title: Choosing, fixing and testing wicks
objectives: Describe the main wick types and what a wick tab does
Fix a wick so it stays upright and centred while wax sets
Run a burn test and record melt pool, flame height and smoke
Decide from test results whether to go up or down a wick size

blocks.text: The wick decides how a candle behaves more than any other part. The same wax in the same jar can burn beautifully with one wick and badly with another. A wick that is **too small** makes a narrow melt pool, so the candle burns a tunnel down the middle and wastes the wax on the sides. A wick that is **too big** makes a tall flame, smoke and soot, and can make a glass jar dangerously hot.
The common wick types

items: **Flat braided cotton wicks**: plaited like hair, they curl slightly as they burn. Often used in pillars and tapers.
**Square braided cotton wicks**: thicker and rounder, popular for beeswax and pillar candles.
**Cored wicks**: a cotton wick with a stiffer centre that helps it stand up straight in container candles and tealights. Buy from a supplier who states what the core is made of.
**Wooden wicks**: thin strips of wood that crackle softly. They need their own size chart and practice.

blocks.text: Most container and tealight wicks are sold **pre-tabbed**: a small metal disc called a **wick tab** (or sustainer) is clamped to the bottom. The tab holds the wick in place and stops the flame before it reaches the base of the jar, which protects the glass. Every supplier publishes a **size chart** that matches wick sizes to wax type and container diameter. Use the chart as your starting point, then test. Charts are a guide, not a promise, because your fragrance, dye and jar shape all change the result.

blocks.name: creative-experiment
blocks.alt: A woman testing samples at a work table
blocks.caption: Treat every new jar, wax or fragrance as an experiment and test the wick before you sell.

blocks.text: Fixing a wick in a jar

items: Wipe the inside of the jar clean and dry. Dust and grease stop the tab from sticking.
Measure the jar's inside diameter at its widest point with a ruler and write it down. This is the number you look up in the wick chart.
Put a wick sticker or a small dot of melted wax on the bottom of the tab and press it to the exact centre of the jar with a pencil or chopstick.
Pull the wick upright and hold it centred with a wick bar, a clothes peg, or two pencils with a rubber band across the jar mouth.
Leave the wick holder in place until the wax is completely set.

blocks.text: The burn test

A burn test is how you prove that your candle is safe and works well. Make at least two test candles with the same wax, fragrance and wick. Let them cure as your wax supplier advises. Then burn one in a still room, on a heat-proof surface, away from fans, open windows and anything that can burn, and stay in the room the whole time.

blocks.title: Burn test routine
items: Trim wick and light
Check every hour
Measure melt pool
Note flame and smoke
Decide wick change
blocks.caption: Change only one thing at a time, so you know what caused the difference.

blocks.text: At each check, write down the time, the flame height, the width of the melt pool, any smoke or soot, and whether the glass feels too hot to hold comfortably near the top. For a container candle, a good result is a melt pool that reaches close to the edge of the jar within a few hours, a calm flame, and no black smoke. Keep the trimmed wick short: the National Candle Association advises trimming wicks to a quarter of an inch (about 6 mm) before each use to prevent high flames and soot.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a burn test log
blocks.context: For example, Folake in Ibadan makes candles in a jar with an inside diameter of 7.5 cm. She tests two wick sizes from her supplier's chart, one size apart, called size A (smaller) and size B (larger).
steps: After 1 hour, wick A has a melt pool 4.0 cm wide; wick B has a melt pool 5.5 cm wide.
After 2 hours, wick A has 5.5 cm; wick B has 7.0 cm and its flame is calm.
After 3 hours, wick A is still 1 cm short of the edge on each side: 7.5 cm minus 5.5 cm leaves 2.0 cm of solid wax across the jar, so it is starting to tunnel.
Wick B reached 7.0 cm at 2 hours, leaving only 0.5 cm, and closes to the edge by hour 3 with no smoke.
She checks wick B's jar near the rim by touch with the back of her hand: warm, not too hot to hold.
blocks.result: Wick B is the right choice for this jar, wax and fragrance. Folake writes the jar size, wax, fragrance load and wick B in her recipe card so every future batch uses the same combination.

head: What you see
Likely meaning
Next test
rows: Tall flame, smoke, soot on glass
Wick too large or too long
Trim, then try one size smaller
Wick too small or too much fragrance
Larger wick, or check fragrance load
Calm flame, full pool, warm glass
Repeat the test on a second candle

blocks.title: Testing safely
blocks.text: Never leave a test candle burning while you sleep or go out. Burn it on a metal tray or ceramic plate. To put it out, use a snuffer or blow gently, never water, which makes hot wax spit. Stop burning a container candle when about 1.3 cm (half an inch) of wax is left, as the National Candle Association advises.

takeaways: Wick size, not wax, causes most burning problems
Start with the supplier's chart for your wax and jar diameter, then burn test
Record melt pool width, flame and smoke at every hourly check
Change one thing at a time and save the winning combination as a recipe card

activity.title: Run your first burn test
steps: Measure the inside diameter of the jar you plan to sell in
Choose two wick sizes next to each other on your supplier's chart
Make one test candle with each wick and let them cure
Burn them side by side for three hours while you stay in the room, recording the pool width every hour
Choose the better wick and write a recipe card
activity.evidence: Your burn test log sheet and a photo of both melt pools at the final check

quiz.q: Bisi's candle keeps burning because liquid wax travels up the wick to the flame. What is this movement called?
quiz.explain: Capillary action is how the wick draws liquid wax up through the tiny gaps in its fibres.

quiz.q: Ada is melting wax and the doorbell rings. What should she do?
options: Turn the heat down and go quickly
Ask a child to watch the pot
Switch off the heat before leaving the cooker
Cover the pot with a towel
quiz.explain: Melting wax must never be left unattended. Switch off the heat first.

quiz.q: Wax in a pot catches fire. Which action is correct?
options: Pour a cup of water on it
Turn off the heat if safe and smother it with a metal lid or fire blanket
Fan the flames to cool them
quiz.explain: Smothering cuts off oxygen. Water turns to steam and throws burning wax out; moving the pot spreads the fire.

quiz.q: Why does a double boiler make melting wax safer?
options: The water keeps the wax from getting hotter than boiling water
It adds moisture to the wax
It removes the need for a thermometer
quiz.explain: Indirect heat through water limits the temperature, protecting the wax and lowering fire risk. You still need a thermometer.

quiz.q: A test candle in an 8 cm jar has a 5 cm melt pool after three hours and is tunnelling. What should Kemi test next?
options: Pouring at a lower temperature only
quiz.explain: A narrow pool and tunnelling usually mean the wick is too small for the diameter.

quiz.q: Which wax is mostly sold for container candles because it is soft?
quiz.explain: Most soy wax is soft and designed for jars rather than freestanding candles.

modules.title: Container, Pillar and Small Candle Production
modules.overview: Make the three product families that most candle businesses sell: scented jar candles, freestanding pillars, and tealights and votives for events. You will calculate quantities, follow each method and keep batch records.

lessons.title: Making a scented container candle from start to finish
objectives: Find the exact wax weight a jar holds with a test pour
Calculate wax and fragrance for a batch, including a small allowance for loss
Follow a container candle method from preparing jars to curing
Keep a batch record that lets you repeat a good result

blocks.text: Container candles are poured into glass jars, tins or ceramic cups and burn inside them. They are the best first product to sell: the jar holds the wax, so you can use soft container wax, the candle cannot fall over, and customers like them as gifts. In this lesson you will make a batch of 12 scented jar candles, using numbers you work out yourself rather than guesses.

blocks.name: jar
blocks.caption: Choose a jar made for candles: thick, heat-resistant glass with no cracks or chips.

blocks.text: Step 1: Find out how much wax one jar holds

Wax does not weigh the same as water, and every jar is different, so the most accurate method is a **test pour**. Weigh an empty, clean jar on a digital kitchen scale. Melt some wax, pour it to the fill line you want (usually about 1 to 1.5 cm below the rim, so the flame sits inside the glass), and let it set completely. Weigh the jar again. The difference is the wax one jar holds. Write it on your recipe card; you only need to do this once per jar style.
Step 2: Calculate the batch

Multiply the wax per jar by the number of jars. Then add about 5 percent extra, because some wax always stays on the jug and spoon. **Fragrance load** is the amount of fragrance oil, written as a percentage of the wax weight. Your wax supplier's data sheet gives a maximum: never go above it, because extra oil can leak out of the candle (called sweating) and can make it burn unsafely. Many makers test a lower load first and only go higher if the scent is weak.

blocks.title: Worked example: a batch of 12 jars
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kaduna has 12 identical jars. Her test pour showed the empty jar weighs 210 g and the filled jar weighs 390 g. Her wax data sheet allows the fragrance load she wants to use, and she chooses 6 percent.
steps: Wax per jar: 390 g minus 210 g = 180 g.
Wax for 12 jars: 12 x 180 g = 2,160 g.
Add 5 percent for loss: 2,160 g x 1.05 = 2,268 g of wax to melt.
Fragrance at 6 percent of the wax melted: 2,268 g x 0.06 = 136.08 g, so she weighs out 136 g of fragrance oil.
She writes all four numbers on her batch sheet before she switches on the cooker.
blocks.result: Halima melts 2,268 g of wax and adds 136 g of fragrance oil. She has enough to fill all 12 jars to the line, with a little left for topping up.

blocks.text: Step 3: The method

items: Wash and dry the jars well. Fix a pre-tabbed wick in the centre of each one and hold it upright with a wick bar or peg.
Warm the jars slightly by standing them in a warm place (not in water). Cold glass can make wax pull away from the sides.
Melt the weighed wax in your double boiler, checking the thermometer, until it reaches the melting temperature on the data sheet.
Add dye if you are using it, and stir until no streaks remain.
Let the wax cool to the fragrance temperature on the data sheet, add the weighed fragrance oil, and stir gently and steadily for about two minutes so it fully mixes in.
When the wax reaches the pouring temperature on the data sheet, pour slowly into each jar to the fill line, keeping the wick centred.
Leave the jars to cool undisturbed in a room without draughts. Do not move them or put them in a fridge.

blocks.title: Container candle method
items: Prepare jars and wicks
Melt wax to temperature
Add dye then fragrance
Pour at pouring temperature
Cool, top up, cure
blocks.caption: Each stage has its own temperature, so the thermometer stays in the jug all the way through.

blocks.text: Step 4: Finish and cure

As wax cools it shrinks, and you may see a dip or small holes around the wick. Reheat a little of the leftover wax and pour a thin top-up layer to make the surface flat. When the candle is completely hard, trim the wick to about 6 mm. Then let the candles **cure**: rest with lids on, at room temperature, so the fragrance settles into the wax. Curing time depends on the wax, so follow the supplier's advice.

head: Batch record item
Halima's entry
rows: Wick B from her burn test

blocks.title: Fragrance oil and heat
blocks.text: Fragrance oil can be flammable and can irritate skin. Wear gloves when you measure it, wipe spills at once, and keep the bottle away from the cooker flame. Read the Safety Data Sheet your supplier provides for each oil and follow its storage advice.

blocks.title: Use a batch code
blocks.text: Write the batch code on the bottom of each jar with a small sticker. If a customer has a problem, you can find exactly how that candle was made.

takeaways: A test pour gives the true wax weight for your jar
Wax for a batch = wax per jar x number of jars, plus about 5 percent for loss
Fragrance weight = wax weight x fragrance load, never above the supplier's maximum
Follow the data sheet's temperatures, top up sinkholes, and cure before selling

activity.title: Pour your first batch of six
steps: Do a test pour to find the wax weight of your jar
Calculate wax and fragrance for six jars on a batch sheet, including 5 percent extra
Make the six candles using your tested wick
Top up any sinkholes and trim the wicks
Label each jar with a batch code and set them to cure
activity.evidence: Your completed batch sheet with calculations and a photo of the six finished candles

lessons.title: Pillar candles: moulds, second pours and clean unmoulding
objectives: Prepare a pillar mould, including threading and sealing the wick
Estimate how much wax to melt using a water fill test
Fix shrinkage with relief holes and a second pour
Unmould and level a pillar candle so it stands straight

blocks.text: A pillar candle stands on its own without a jar. That means the wax must be hard enough to hold its shape when warm, so you use a **pillar grade wax** (a harder paraffin, palm wax, beeswax or a blend made for pillars), not soft container wax. Pillars are popular for church use, table settings, events and gift sets, and a neat, smooth pillar looks very professional.
Choosing a mould

items: **Metal moulds** (aluminium): last for years and give a smooth, shiny finish. They have a small hole at the bottom for the wick.
**Plastic or polycarbonate moulds**: cheaper and show you the wax through the side, but can be damaged if the wax is hotter than the mould maker allows.
**Silicone moulds**: bend away from the candle, so they are good for shapes such as spheres, cubes and flowers. You push the wick through with a wicking needle.
**Home-made moulds** such as clean cardboard tubes lined with baking paper work for tests, but are hard to make perfectly round.

blocks.text: Remember that the **bottom of the mould becomes the top of the candle**. The wick goes through the hole at the base of the mould, and is tied or clipped across the open end, which becomes the candle's base.
Preparing the mould

items: Clean and dry the mould. Any old wax or dust shows on the finished surface.
Thread a pillar wick (not pre-tabbed) through the hole in the base, leaving a few centimetres outside.
Seal the hole from the outside with mould sealer putty so no wax leaks out. Press it firmly around the wick.
Pull the wick straight and tie it to a wick bar or pencil resting across the open end, exactly in the centre.
If your mould maker recommends it, wipe the inside with a very thin film of mould release. Silicone moulds usually do not need it.
Stand the mould on a tray on a level surface.

blocks.name: artist-at-work
blocks.alt: A maker working carefully at a bench
blocks.caption: Pillar work rewards patience: a straight wick and slow cooling give the cleanest result.

blocks.text: How much wax to melt

Before your first pour, seal the mould, fill it with water up to the line you want, and weigh the water. A gram of water is about a millilitre, so this tells you the mould's volume. Candle wax is lighter than water, so the wax that fills the same space weighs **less** than the water did. If you melt the same number of grams of wax as the water weighed, you will have enough, with some extra for the second pour. Dry the mould completely before using it for wax.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 7 cm by 10 cm pillar
blocks.context: For example, Ruth in Jos has an aluminium cylinder mould. She fills it with water to 10 cm high, and the water weighs 385 g.
steps: Because wax is lighter than water, 385 g of wax will more than fill the mould. She rounds up and melts 400 g of pillar wax to have enough for both pours.
She uses a 5 percent fragrance load, within her pillar wax data sheet's maximum: 400 g x 0.05 = 20 g of fragrance oil.
She keeps about 60 g of the scented wax back in the jug for the second pour, so the first pour is about 400 g minus 60 g = 340 g.
When a firm skin forms on top, she pokes two or three relief holes near the wick with a skewer to let trapped air out.
Once the candle has shrunk and a dip forms around the wick, she reheats the reserved wax and fills the dip, stopping at the level of the first pour.
blocks.result: The second pour fills the cavity so the base is flat and solid. Ruth records 400 g melted and 60 g reserved on her recipe card for this mould.

blocks.title: One pillar, from pour to finish
items: First pour
Skin forms
Poke relief holes
Second pour
Fully cool
Unmould and level
blocks.caption: Shrinkage is normal in pillars; the relief holes and second pour are part of the method, not a repair.

blocks.text: Unmoulding and finishing

Wait until the candle is completely cool all the way through. This can take many hours for a large pillar. Remove the putty and untie the wick. A candle that is fully cool shrinks slightly from the mould walls and slides out easily; if it sticks, it usually needs more time. Never force it with a knife, which scratches both mould and candle.

To level the base, rub it gently in small circles on a clean metal tray warmed over your double boiler until the bottom is flat, then let it harden. Trim the wick at the top to about 6 mm. Polish the sides with a soft cloth or a nylon stocking to remove fingerprints.

blocks.title: Pillars need a holder when burning
blocks.text: Tell customers to burn pillars on a heat-proof plate or pillar holder, because some wax can run down the side. The National Candle Association advises keeping burning candles at least 30 cm (12 inches) from anything that can burn, and putting them out before leaving the room or going to bed.

head: Problem
Cause
Fix next time
rows: No relief holes or second pour
Poke relief holes and always do a second pour
Wick not pulled tight or bar moved
Tie the wick firmly and check it after pouring
Press putty all round the wick and test with water first
Not cool enough or no release
Wait longer; use release if the mould maker recommends it

takeaways: Pillars need harder, pillar grade wax
The mould's base becomes the candle's top
A water fill test tells you how much wax to melt
Relief holes and a second pour are normal steps for every pillar

activity.title: Make and unmould one pillar
steps: Do a water fill test on your mould and write down the weight
Thread, seal and centre the wick
Pour the first layer, keeping some wax back
Poke relief holes, then do the second pour
Unmould when completely cool, level the base and trim the wick
activity.evidence: Photos of the mould set-up, the second pour, and the finished pillar standing straight

lessons.title: Tealights, votives and decorative candles for events
objectives: Explain the difference between tealights and votives and how each is burned
Plan a large tealight order with correct wax quantities
Make layered and colour-graded candles
Decorate candles without adding fire risks

blocks.text: Small candles sell in quantity. Hosts buy them by the dozen for weddings, naming ceremonies, birthdays, church services and restaurant tables. They use little wax each, so they are cheap to make, but they must be identical, burn safely and be ready on the day promised. This lesson shows you how to produce them in batches, and how to add decorative styles that make your table candles stand out.

blocks.title: Tealight vs votive
items: Tealight
Votive
blocks.caption: Both are small, but a votive must always be sold or used with a holder.

blocks.text: Making tealights in bulk

items: Buy empty tealight cups (aluminium or clear plastic made for candles) and pre-tabbed tealight wicks that match your supplier's chart.
Do a test pour to find how much wax one cup holds, as you did for jars.
Set the cups out in rows on a tray, close together, so you can pour along a line.
Place a wick tab in the centre of each cup. Many tealight wicks stand on their own; if not, press the tab down with a pencil.
Pour from a jug with a narrow spout, filling each cup just below the rim. Re-centre any wick that tilts while the wax is still liquid.
Leave to set, then top up any dips with a little reheated wax.

blocks.title: Worked example: 48 tealights for a naming ceremony
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Benin City receives an order for 48 unscented white tealights for a naming ceremony on Saturday. Her test pour showed one cup holds 14 g of wax.
steps: Wax needed: 48 x 14 g = 672 g.
Add 5 percent for loss: 672 g x 1.05 = 705.6 g, so she melts about 706 g.
Unscented is better for food tables, so she adds no fragrance oil.
She makes 50, not 48, so she can keep two for a short burn test before delivery.
She pours on Wednesday, giving time to set, top up, test and pack before Saturday.
blocks.result: Grace delivers 48 identical tealights with a day to spare, and her two test candles confirm they burn cleanly.

blocks.name: celebration
blocks.caption: Events need many identical candles delivered on time, so plan quantities and dates backwards from the event.

blocks.text: Votives

Votives are made in small metal votive moulds, using a wick with its own small tab, and a wax suitable for votives. When burned, a well-wicked votive melts completely and becomes a pool of liquid wax, so it must burn in a glass or metal holder only slightly larger than the candle. Tell customers this clearly: a votive on a bare plate will spread hot wax across the table.
Decorative techniques

items: **Layered candles**: pour one colour, let it set until the surface is firm but still warm, then pour the next colour. Pouring too early makes the colours mix; waiting until the first layer is cold can make the layers separate.
**Ombre (colour grading)**: start with lightly coloured wax for the first layer, then add a little more dye to the jug before each next layer, so the colour deepens from bottom to top.
**Wax chunk candles**: pour coloured pillar wax into a tray, cut the hardened wax into cubes, place them in a mould, and pour clear or white wax over them.
**Tilted layers**: prop jars at an angle with a folded towel while each layer sets for a slanted stripe effect.

blocks.title: Keep decorations away from the flame
blocks.text: Dried flowers, leaves, herbs, paper, ribbons and glitter can catch fire. Do not put them in the wax that the flame will reach. Decorate the **outside** of the jar, the lid, the label or the gift box instead. Keep coloured wax chunks and dye as your decoration inside the candle.

Colour is easy to overdo. Liquid wax always looks darker than it will when set, and too much dye can affect how a candle burns. Add a small amount, stir, then drip a little on a white saucer to see the true colour once it cools. Write down exactly how many chips or drops gave the shade you want so the next batch matches.

Before you accept an event order, ask the host four questions in writing: how many candles, what colour and scent (or unscented), the delivery date and address, and whether the venue allows open flames. Some halls and hotels have their own rules about candles, and it is better to know before you pour. Agree the price and deposit in the same message so there is a clear record.

head: Order type
Plan this many extra
Why
rows: Burn test before delivery and spares for breakage
Some cups tip or wicks lean
Check colours match the client's sample

takeaways: Tealights burn in their own cup; votives must burn in a holder
Plan large orders with a test pour, then add 5 percent wax and a few spare candles
Layer timing matters: firm but warm surfaces give clean lines
Flammable decorations belong on the outside of the candle, never in the burning wax

activity.title: Plan and pour a mini event order
steps: Do a test pour for one tealight cup
Calculate wax for 24 tealights with 5 percent extra
Pour 26 tealights (24 plus 2 for testing)
Burn one test tealight completely while you stay in the room, and note the burn time
Pack the 24 neatly as if for delivery
activity.evidence: Your calculation, the burn time note and a photo of the packed order

quiz.q: Halima's empty jar weighs 200 g and the filled, set jar weighs 350 g. How much wax does one jar hold?
quiz.explain: Wax per jar is filled weight minus empty weight: 350 g minus 200 g = 150 g.

quiz.q: Ifeoma will melt 1,500 g of wax and wants a 6 percent fragrance load. How much fragrance oil does she weigh?
quiz.explain: 1,500 g x 0.06 = 90 g. Check that 6 percent is within the supplier's maximum.

quiz.q: Why do pillar candles need relief holes and a second pour?
options: Wax shrinks as it cools and leaves holes near the wick
quiz.explain: Cooling wax shrinks and forms cavities; relief holes and a second pour fill them.

quiz.q: Which decoration is safe to put inside the wax of a burning candle?
quiz.explain: Wax chunks burn like the rest of the candle. Petals, paper and glitter can catch fire.

quiz.q: A customer will burn votives on a bare plate. What should you tell her?
options: Burn them in a holder slightly larger than the candle, because they melt completely
Burn them only for one hour
quiz.explain: A well-made votive becomes liquid as it burns, so it needs a holder.

quiz.q: Which wax should Ruth use for a freestanding pillar?
options: Any wax, it does not matter
quiz.explain: Pillars need a harder wax made for freestanding candles so they hold their shape.

modules.title: Fragrance, Colour and Troubleshooting
modules.overview: Choose and blend fragrances that sell, colour wax evenly, and fix the faults every candle maker meets. You will learn to test with evidence and use batch records to answer customers.

lessons.title: Scent and colour: choosing oils, blending and dyeing
objectives: Explain the difference between candle fragrance oils and essential oils
Describe top, middle and base notes and use them to plan a blend
Scale a small test blend up to a full batch using percentages
Colour wax evenly with candle dyes and record the recipe

blocks.text: Many customers pick up a candle, smell it, and decide in seconds. Two words describe what they notice. **Cold throw** is how strong the candle smells before it is lit. **Hot throw** is how well the scent fills a room while it burns. A good candle has both. You control them through the oil you choose, the fragrance load, the temperature you add it at, and the cure time.
Fragrance oils and essential oils

head: Candle fragrance oil
Essential oil
rows: A blend of aroma materials made for candles
A concentrated oil taken from a plant
Very wide: vanilla, coconut, fresh linen, oud styles
Only what plants give: lemongrass, orange, eucalyptus, lavender
Usually designed to throw well when burned
Often weaker when burned, and some fade quickly
Supplier should give a Safety Data Sheet
Supplier should give a Safety Data Sheet

blocks.text: Buy oils described as **suitable for candles** from a supplier who can give you the **Safety Data Sheet (SDS)** for each one. The SDS tells you how to store and handle the oil and its flash point. Many international fragrance suppliers also provide an IFRA certificate, which states the maximum amount of that fragrance that may be used in each type of product, including candles. Keep these papers in a folder; serious buyers such as hotels may ask for them. Never use perfume, body spray or cooking flavourings in candles: they are not made to burn.

blocks.name: lotion-bottle
blocks.caption: Keep every fragrance bottle labelled, capped and away from the cooker, with its data sheet on file.

blocks.text: Building a blend with notes

Perfumers describe a scent in three layers called **notes**. Top notes are the bright smells you notice first, such as lemon, orange, lemongrass and mint; they fade fastest. Middle notes are the heart of the scent, often floral or spicy, such as rose, jasmine, cinnamon or ginger. Base notes are deep and long-lasting, such as vanilla, sandalwood, amber, musk or oud. A balanced blend uses some of each, usually with less of the strongest base note.

blocks.title: The fragrance pyramid
items: Top: citrus, lemongrass, mint
Middle: florals, spices
Base: vanilla, woods, musk
blocks.caption: Top notes greet the customer, middle notes carry the scent, base notes make it last.

blocks.text: Test small, then scale up

items: Decide your blend as parts out of 10, for example 5 parts top, 3 parts middle, 2 parts base.
Mix a small test blend by weight in a clean glass bottle, for example 5 g, 3 g and 2 g, making 10 g.
Close the bottle, label it, and let it rest for a day or two so the oils settle together.
Dip a strip of plain paper, let it dry for a minute, and smell it. Ask two or three other people too.
Adjust the parts, then make one or two test candles before you change your full recipe.
Scale up by turning the parts into percentages of the total fragrance weight.

blocks.title: Worked example: scaling a blend to a full batch
blocks.context: For example, Blessing in Port Harcourt likes her test blend of lemongrass (top), ginger (middle) and vanilla (base) in the ratio 5 : 3 : 2. She will melt 1,500 g of container wax at a 6 percent fragrance load, which is within her data sheet maximum.
steps: Total fragrance: 1,500 g x 0.06 = 90 g.
5 : 3 : 2 adds up to 10 parts, so the shares are 50 percent, 30 percent and 20 percent.
Lemongrass: 90 g x 0.50 = 45 g.
Ginger: 90 g x 0.30 = 27 g.
Vanilla: 90 g x 0.20 = 18 g.
Check: 45 g + 27 g + 18 g = 90 g.
blocks.result: Blessing weighs 45 g, 27 g and 18 g into one jug, stirs them together, and adds the 90 g blend at the fragrance temperature on her wax data sheet. She names it 'Garden Fresh' and saves the recipe.

blocks.title: More fragrance is not always better
blocks.text: Going above the supplier's maximum does not reliably make a stronger candle. Extra oil can seep to the surface, make the flame smoky, or create a fire risk. If the scent is weak, check your wick, the temperature you added the oil, and your cure time before adding more.
Colouring wax

items: Use **candle dyes**: dye chips or blocks, liquid candle dye, or dye flakes. They are made to dissolve in wax.
Do not use crayons, paint or pigment powders meant for other crafts; the particles can clog the wick and make it smoke.
Do not use food colouring: it is water-based and will not mix with wax.
Add dye before fragrance, when the wax is fully melted, and stir until no streaks remain.
Drip a little coloured wax on a white saucer to see the true set colour before you pour.

blocks.text: Dye fades in strong sunlight, so display coloured candles out of direct sun and tell customers the same. Record exactly what you used, for example '2 chips of green per 1,000 g of wax', so you can match the colour every time. Matching colour is especially important for event orders where 50 candles must look the same.

takeaways: Cold throw is scent before lighting; hot throw is scent while burning
Use oils made for candles and keep each Safety Data Sheet
Plan blends in parts, test small, then scale up with percentages
Use candle dye only, and record amounts so colours match

activity.title: Create and scale your signature blend
steps: Choose one top, one middle and one base note you can buy locally
Mix a 10 g test blend in parts and let it rest
Do the paper strip test with three people and note their comments
Calculate the weight of each oil for a 1,000 g wax batch at your chosen load
Make one test candle with the blend
activity.evidence: Your blend recipe card with parts, percentages and grams, plus the testers' comments

lessons.title: Diagnosing and fixing common candle faults
objectives: Recognise the most common candle faults by how they look
Link each fault to its most likely cause
Choose a single change to test, and confirm the fix with a burn test
Use batch records to answer a customer complaint

blocks.text: Every candle maker gets faults. The difference between a hobby and a business is what you do next. A professional looks at the candle, checks the batch record, changes **one thing**, and tests again. This lesson gives you a fault guide and a routine to follow, so you fix problems with evidence instead of guessing.
Faults you can see while burning

head: Fault
What it looks like
Most likely cause
What to change
rows: Deep hole down the middle, wax left on the sides
Wick too small; or first burn too short
Test one wick size up; tell customers to let the first burn melt to the edges
A black carbon blob on the wick tip
Wick too large or not trimmed; heavy fragrance or dye
Trim to about 6 mm before each burn; test a smaller wick
Black smoke, dark marks on the glass
Wick too long or too big, draught, or crafts dye
Trim, move away from fans and windows, check wick and dye
Flame shrinks and goes out in the pool
Wick too small, or too much fragrance oil
Larger wick, or reduce fragrance within the supplier range
Fragrance added too hot or too cold, short cure, small pool
Follow data sheet temperatures, cure longer, check wick

blocks.text: Faults you can see before lighting

head: Fault
What it looks like
Most likely cause
What to change
rows: Dip or holes near the wick
Top-up pour; relief holes for pillars
Patches where wax has pulled away from the glass
Cold jars, draughts, or fast cooling
Warm jars slightly, cool slowly away from draughts. Mostly a looks problem
Fragrance above what the wax can hold, or heat in storage
White powdery look, common in soy wax
Pour at the data sheet temperature; accept a little in natural waxes
Cooling too fast, such as in a fridge or draught

blocks.name: taking-notes
blocks.alt: A woman writing notes at a desk
blocks.caption: Your batch records turn every fault into information you can act on.

blocks.text: The fix routine

blocks.title: Before you change a recipe
items: Photo of the fault
Batch record checked
One likely cause chosen
One change made
Burn test repeated
Recipe card updated
blocks.caption: Changing two things at once means you will never know which one worked.

blocks.text: Start by taking a clear photo of the fault and noting the batch code. Read the batch record: wax, fragrance load, temperatures, wick, cure time and weather. Look for anything that was different from your good batches. Choose the most likely cause from the tables, change only that one thing, and make two new test candles. Burn test them as you learned in Module 1. When the fault is gone, update your recipe card and note the date of the change.

blocks.title: Worked example: a customer complaint
blocks.context: For example, Nkechi in Abuja sells a jar candle called 'Warm Vanilla'. A customer sends a WhatsApp photo: after the third burn, there is a deep tunnel and the flame is small. The batch code on the base is NK-14.
steps: Nkechi thanks the customer and asks one question: how long did the first burn last? The answer: about 40 minutes.
She checks batch NK-14: same wax, wick and fragrance as earlier batches, but she had switched to a wider jar (8.5 cm instead of 7.5 cm) because her usual jar was out of stock.
The wider jar means the old wick is probably too small, and the short first burn made it worse.
She makes two test candles in the new jar, one with the old wick and one with the next size up, and burns them side by side.
The larger wick reaches the edge in about 3 hours; the old one leaves about 1.5 cm of solid wax on each side.
blocks.result: Nkechi replaces the customer's candle, uses the larger wick for all 8.5 cm jars, and adds a line to her label: 'First burn: let the wax melt to the edges.' She also adds 'any change of jar = new burn test' to her rules.

blocks.title: When a fault is a safety problem
blocks.text: Some faults are only about looks: wet spots, frosting, small surface marks. Others are safety issues: very high flames, heavy smoke, a glass that gets too hot to touch, or a jar that cracks. Stop selling that batch until you have found the cause and tested a fix. Never sell a candle you would not burn in your own home.

Teach customers to use candles well, because many complaints come from use, not making. Your care card can say: let the first burn melt the wax to the edge, trim the wick before each use, keep the candle away from fans and open windows, and never leave it burning in an empty room. A short, friendly reply that explains this, together with a replacement when the fault was yours, keeps customers loyal.

takeaways: Most burning faults trace back to wick size, trimming or fragrance load
Wet spots and frosting are mostly cosmetic; high flames, heavy smoke and hot glass are safety faults
Fix one cause at a time and confirm with a burn test
Batch codes and records let you answer complaints with facts

activity.title: Build your fault file
steps: Burn one of your own candles for three hours while you stay in the room
Photograph the surface before lighting and the melt pool at the end
Name any fault you see using the tables in this lesson
Write the likely cause and the one change you would test
Draft a three-line care card for customers
activity.evidence: A one-page fault file with photos, your diagnosis, and your care card text

quiz.q: A candle has a black blob on the wick tip and soot on the glass. What is the most likely cause?
quiz.explain: Mushrooming and soot usually point to a wick that is too big or too long.

quiz.q: Blessing's blend is 5 : 3 : 2 and she needs 120 g of fragrance in total. How much of the base note (2 parts) does she need?
quiz.explain: 2 parts out of 10 is 20 percent: 120 g x 0.20 = 24 g.

quiz.q: What is 'hot throw'?
options: How well the scent fills a room while the candle burns
The scent of the unlit candle
quiz.explain: Hot throw is scent while burning; cold throw is scent before lighting.

quiz.q: Which of these should never be used to colour candle wax?
quiz.explain: Food colouring is water-based and will not mix with wax. Crayons and craft paints can clog the wick.

quiz.q: Nkechi's candles tunnel after she changed to a wider jar. What should she do first?
options: Change the wax, wick and jar together
Burn test the new jar with the old wick and one size larger
quiz.explain: Change one thing at a time. A wider jar usually needs a larger wick, which a side-by-side burn test confirms.

quiz.q: Which fault is a safety problem that means you stop selling the batch?
options: A small wet spot on the glass
Glass that becomes too hot to touch while burning
quiz.explain: Overheating glass can crack. Frosting, wet spots and colour variation are cosmetic.

modules.title: Packaging, Pricing and Your Candle Business
modules.overview: Turn good candles into a trusted product line. You will write honest labels, test burn time, choose packaging for each type of buyer, cost and price a batch, and sell safely through the channels that suit candles.

lessons.title: Labels, burn-time testing and packaging that sells
objectives: Write a candle label with the information buyers and safety require
Measure burn time honestly with a timed test
Choose packaging that suits household, gift and event customers
Pack candles so they survive heat and delivery

blocks.text: Your label is where a customer decides whether to trust you. It must tell her what she is buying, how to use it safely, and how to reach you. A clean, honest label also makes your candles easier to sell to shops, hotels and event planners, who need to know exactly what they are stocking.
What goes on a candle label

items: **Brand name and logo**, the same on every product.
**Product name and scent**, for example 'Garden Fresh: lemongrass, ginger and vanilla'.
**Net weight of wax** in grams, from your test pour (not the weight of the jar).
**Wax type**, described honestly. Only say '100% soy' if the wax really is 100 percent soy.
**Approximate burn time**, from your own timed test.
**Batch code** and your **phone or WhatsApp number**.
**Safety and care instructions**, either on the label or on a small card.

blocks.title: Safety wording you can use
blocks.text: Based on National Candle Association guidance: Never leave a burning candle unattended. Keep out of reach of children and pets. Keep at least 30 cm (12 inches) from anything that can burn. Trim the wick to about 6 mm (1/4 inch) before each use. Stop using when about 1.3 cm (1/2 inch) of wax remains. Put out with a snuffer or by blowing gently, never with water.
Testing burn time

Do not guess burn time or copy it from another brand. Take two finished, cured candles from the same batch. Burn each in sessions of a few hours, in a still room, while you stay with it. Write the start and stop time of every session. Trim the wick before each session. Stop when about 1.3 cm of wax remains, then add up the hours. Use the **lower** of the two results and round down, so customers get at least what you promise.

blocks.title: Worked example: burn time for a 180 g jar
blocks.context: For example, Halima tests two candles from batch HK-07 over one week, burning them while she works at home.
steps: Candle 1 sessions: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 2.5 + 2 hours = 16.5 hours.
Candle 2 sessions: 3 + 3 + 3.5 + 3 + 2.5 + 2 hours = 17 hours.
She takes the lower result, 16.5 hours, and rounds down.
Her label says 'Burn time: about 16 hours'.
blocks.result: Every customer's candle should last at least as long as the label says, so Halima's claim is honest and she has a written test log to back it up.

blocks.title: Label check before printing
items: Brand and product name
Net wax weight
Honest wax description
Tested burn time
Batch code and contact
Safety instructions
blocks.caption: If any line is missing or untested, fix it before you print a full roll of labels.

blocks.text: Packaging for different buyers

head: Customer
Packaging idea
What matters most
rows: Jar with a printed sticker and a lid
Clear scent name, fair price, safety text
Box with paper filling, a ribbon outside the box, a care card
Matching sets, custom label with names and date
Every piece identical, delivered on time
Plain pillars or tealights packed in dozens
Consistent size, easy counting, reliable supply
Simple, clean jar, possibly with their name

blocks.name: gift-box
blocks.caption: Gift packaging lets you serve the birthday, wedding and festive seasons with the same candle.

blocks.text: Candles soften in heat. Store finished stock in a cool, shaded room, never in a hot car boot or in direct sun at a market stall. For delivery, wrap each jar in paper, stand it upright in a box with padding so it cannot knock its neighbour, and mark the box 'Fragile, keep upright, keep cool'. Ask dispatch riders not to leave parcels in the sun.
Where the label goes and how it looks

Put the brand, product name and scent on the front, where a buyer sees them first on a shelf or in a photo. Put net weight, burn time, wax type and batch code on the side or back, and the full safety text on the base or on a care card tucked into the box. Choose a label material that does not smudge when touched with oily fingers: a matte paper sticker with a printed or laminated finish works better than plain paper and glue. Keep fonts large enough to read without glasses, and use the same colours and logo on every scent so your products look like one family.

Take product photos in daylight near a window, on a plain background, with the label facing the camera. Show one photo of the candle unlit and one burning with a full, even melt pool, because that second photo quietly tells buyers your wick is right. Use the same photos in your WhatsApp catalogue, on Instagram and on printed price lists so customers recognise your products everywhere.

blocks.title: Registration and bigger buyers
blocks.text: Register your business name with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) when you are ready to sell more widely; it helps when opening a business bank account and dealing with shops. If a supermarket or large buyer asks for further approvals or standards, ask them in writing exactly what they need before you spend money.

takeaways: Label net wax weight, honest wax type, tested burn time, batch code, contact and safety text
Measure burn time on two candles and use the lower, rounded-down result
Match packaging to the buyer: household, gift, event, church or hotel
Keep stock cool and pack upright with padding

activity.title: Design and test your label
steps: Draft your label text with all six items from the checklist
Run a burn-time test on two candles and write the result
Make a simple label design in Canva or by hand
Print or write one label and stick it on a finished candle
Pack that candle as a gift, ready for delivery
activity.evidence: Your burn-time log and a photo of the labelled, packed candle

lessons.title: Costing, pricing and selling your candles
objectives: Calculate the full cost of one candle, including packaging, energy and your labour
Set a retail price with a target profit margin
Work out what you earn on a wholesale order before you agree
Take payments safely and choose the best sales channels

blocks.text: Many makers price candles by looking at what others charge, then discover months later that they were working for free. The safe way is to cost every batch from your own receipts, then add a profit you choose. In this lesson all naira figures are **made-up example prices** to show the method. Prices change often, so always use your own current receipts.
Step 1: Cost the whole batch

List everything that goes into the batch: wax, fragrance, wicks, jars, dye, labels, boxes and the gas or electricity you use. Then add your **labour**: the hours you spend multiplied by a fair hourly rate. If you leave out your own time, your price will be too low to grow the business. Finally, remember the candles you keep for burn tests: they cost money but are not sold.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing Halima's batch of 12 jars
blocks.context: For example, Halima uses her batch HK-07 numbers (2,268 g wax, 136 g fragrance, 12 jars). The prices below are example figures only.
steps: Wax: 2.268 kg x 4,000 naira per kg = 9,072 naira.
Fragrance: 136 g x 30 naira per g = 4,080 naira.
Wicks: 12 x 150 = 1,800 naira. Jars: 12 x 600 = 7,200 naira.
Dye 300 naira; labels 12 x 100 = 1,200 naira; gift boxes 12 x 250 = 3,000 naira; gas 800 naira.
Labour: 4 hours x 1,000 naira = 4,000 naira. Batch total: 27,452 + 4,000 = 31,452 naira.
She keeps 1 candle for burn testing, so 11 are for sale: 31,452 / 11 = about 2,859 naira per candle.
blocks.result: Each candle Halima sells really costs her about 2,859 naira (example figures). Any price below this loses money, even if the candles sell fast.

blocks.text: Step 2: Set the price with a margin

**Profit margin** is the share of the selling price that is profit. To get a price with a chosen margin, divide the cost by (1 minus the margin). For a 40 percent margin: 2,859 / 0.60 = about 4,765 naira. Halima rounds up to a clean **4,800 naira**. Her profit per candle is 4,800 minus 2,859 = 1,941 naira, which is about 40 percent of the price. If 11 candles sell, the batch brings in 11 x 4,800 = 52,800 naira, and after the full batch cost of 31,452 naira (which already pays her labour), 21,348 naira is left as profit.

blocks.title: From receipts to price
items: List batch costs
Add labour
Divide by sellable candles
Divide by (1 minus margin)
Round and compare market
blocks.caption: The market check comes last: first know your floor, then see where you fit.

blocks.text: Step 3: Check wholesale and bulk offers

Gift shops and boutiques often ask for a discount so they can resell. Calculate before you agree. At a 25 percent discount, Halima's 4,800 naira candle becomes 4,800 x 0.75 = 3,600 naira. Her profit drops to 3,600 minus 2,859 = 741 naira per candle. That can still be worth it for a large regular order, but not for three candles. Set a minimum order quantity for wholesale prices, and for custom event orders ask for a deposit before you buy materials.

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.caption: Cost every batch on paper or in a spreadsheet before you quote a price.

blocks.text: Where candles sell

items: **WhatsApp Business**: set up a catalogue with photos, prices and scent descriptions, and share Status updates before Valentine's, Mother's Day, Christmas and wedding season.
**Instagram**: short videos of pouring and the finished flame build trust.
**Event planners and decorators**: offer matching tealights, pillars and favours with custom labels.
**Churches**: plain white pillars and tealights in steady quantities.
**Hotels, guesthouses and spas**: a sample candle and a simple price list can open a regular order.
**Gift shops and boutiques**: wholesale or sale-or-return, with a written agreement.

blocks.text: Review your sales record at the end of each month. Note which scents and sizes sold out and which sat on the shelf, and plan your next batches around the winners. Re-cost a product whenever a supplier changes a price, because a small rise in wax or jar prices can wipe out your margin without you noticing. Plan stock early for busy seasons, since candles need time to cure before they are ready to sell.

blocks.title: Payment safety
blocks.text: Before you release goods, confirm that the money has arrived by checking your own bank, Opay or Moniepoint app. Do not rely on a screenshot or an SMS alert sent by the buyer, as fake alerts are a common scam. For online card payments, a payment service such as Paystack sends confirmation to your own dashboard. Keep a simple sales record of date, buyer, item, amount and how paid.

takeaways: Cost the full batch, including packaging, energy, labour and test candles
Price = cost per candle divided by (1 minus your margin), then round
Work out wholesale profit before agreeing to any discount
Release goods only after you see the money in your own account

activity.title: Cost and price one product
steps: Collect your real receipts for one batch
List every cost line and add your labour
Divide by the number of candles you can sell
Calculate retail at a 40 percent margin and wholesale at 25 percent off
Write your price list and post it in your WhatsApp Business catalogue
activity.evidence: Your costing sheet with all calculations and a screenshot of your price list

quiz.q: A batch costs 24,000 naira in total and gives 10 sellable candles. What is the cost per candle?
quiz.explain: 24,000 / 10 = 2,400 naira per candle.

quiz.q: Cost per candle is 3,000 naira. What price gives a 40 percent margin?
quiz.explain: Price = cost / (1 minus margin) = 3,000 / 0.60 = 5,000 naira. Check: profit 2,000 is 40 percent of 5,000.

quiz.q: A shop wants 25 percent off a 4,000 naira candle that costs you 2,500 naira. What is your profit per candle?
quiz.explain: 4,000 x 0.75 = 3,000 naira; 3,000 minus 2,500 = 500 naira profit.

quiz.q: Two burn tests give 18 hours and 19.5 hours. What should the label say?
quiz.explain: Use the lower result and round down so every customer gets at least what you promise.

quiz.q: A buyer sends a screenshot of a transfer and asks you to dispatch now. What should you do?
options: Confirm the money is in your own bank or wallet app first
Accept an SMS alert as proof
quiz.explain: Screenshots and SMS alerts can be faked. Check your own account before releasing goods.

quiz.q: Which line should NOT be on Halima's label if her wax is a soy and paraffin blend?
quiz.explain: Wax descriptions must be honest. A blend cannot be labelled 100 percent soy.

finalQuiz.q: In a burning candle, what carries liquid wax up to the flame?
finalQuiz.explain: The wick draws melted wax upward through its fibres, where the heat turns it to vapour.

finalQuiz.q: Which way of melting wax is correct?
options: A pot of wax directly on the gas flame
A double boiler with a thermometer, never left unattended
Any pot, as long as it is quick
finalQuiz.explain: Indirect heat, a thermometer and constant attention keep wax below dangerous temperatures.

finalQuiz.q: Wax in Joy's jug catches fire. What is the right first action?
options: Turn off the heat if safe and cover with a metal lid or fire blanket
finalQuiz.explain: Smother the fire and cut off oxygen. Water makes burning wax explode out of the pot.

finalQuiz.q: A test candle tunnels and leaves thick wax on the sides. What should be tested next?
finalQuiz.explain: Tunnelling usually means the wick is too small for the jar diameter.

finalQuiz.q: Amaka will melt 2,000 g of wax at an 8 percent fragrance load (within her supplier's maximum). How much fragrance oil?
Each tealight holds 18 g. About how much wax should Grace melt for 20 tealights, with 5 percent extra?
Why is the second pour part of making every pillar candle?
options: To fill the cavity left as wax shrinks while cooling
To make it heavier for the label
finalQuiz.explain: Wax shrinks as it cools; relief holes and a second pour give a solid, flat base.

finalQuiz.q: Where should dried flowers go on a decorative candle?
options: Mixed into the wax around the wick
On the outside of the jar, lid or box
On top of the wax near the wick
finalQuiz.explain: Flowers, paper and glitter can catch fire, so keep them away from the burning wax.

finalQuiz.q: Which colourant is right for candles?
finalQuiz.explain: Candle dyes are made to dissolve in wax. Others can clog the wick or will not mix.

finalQuiz.q: Candle burn tests give 14 and 15 hours. What should the label say?
finalQuiz.explain: Use the lower, rounded-down result so every customer gets at least what you promise.

finalQuiz.q: A candle costs 4,500 naira to make. What price gives a 40 percent margin?
Which is the safest way to accept payment for a candle order?
options: Dispatch after seeing the buyer's screenshot
Dispatch after the buyer's SMS alert
Check the money in your own bank or wallet app first
Deliver first and collect later from new customers
finalQuiz.explain: Screenshots and SMS alerts can be faked. Confirm in your own account.

capstone.title: Launch a tested six-candle product line
capstone.brief: Produce, test, label, cost and present one scented container candle in six jars, ready to sell, with the records that prove it is safe and consistent.
steps: Set up your melting station and photograph it with your fire plan card
Do a test pour and burn test two wick sizes in your chosen jar
Create and scale a fragrance blend, then make six candles with a full batch sheet
Burn test two candles from the batch for burn time and note any faults and fixes
Design and apply labels with net weight, tested burn time, batch code, contact and safety text
Cost the batch, set retail and wholesale prices, and post the product in your WhatsApp Business catalogue
evidence: Photo of the safe melting station
Burn test log with the chosen wick
Batch sheet with wax, fragrance and dye weights
Burn-time log and the label text
Costing sheet with retail and wholesale prices
